planting.note: Set nursery-grown plants into consistently moist, acidic, sandy to peaty soil; avoid letting the planting site dry out during the growing season.

directions: Pine barren gentian is one of the most distinctive and latest-blooming wildflowers of the New Jersey Pinelands, opening its deep blue, funnel-shaped flowers from late September into early winter, long after most other perennials have finished. It occurs naturally in the wet, acidic, sandy soil of open bog margins and pine-savanna swales, conditions that take real effort to recreate in a typical garden bed. Plant into consistently moist, humus-poor, acidic soil in full sun where the water table stays near the surface, and never let the site dry out for extended periods. This is a genuinely challenging species best attempted by experienced native-plant gardeners who can offer bog-like conditions; establishment can be slow and uneven even then.

planting.note: Set plugs or rhizome divisions into saturated to shallowly flooded soil in spring; tolerates brackish tidal flooding once established.

directions: American threesquare gets its name from the sharply triangular, leafless stems that give it a distinctly three-sided profile in cross-section, a useful field mark among bulrushes. It is one of the key marsh-building plants of Chesapeake Bay's tidal shorelines, forming dense colonies that bind sediment across both the brackish lower marsh and the fresher reaches of tidal creeks. Plant divisions or plugs into consistently saturated to shallowly flooded soil in full sun; once established it spreads steadily by thick rhizomes and tolerates periodic tidal inundation as well as brief dry spells. Use it at the water's edge of a rain garden, pond, or living-shoreline planting alongside smooth cordgrass and saltmeadow cordgrass to build a naturalistic marsh transition.

planting.note: Plant tubers or nursery plugs into saturated to tidally flooded soil once the threat of hard freezes has passed.

directions: Saltmarsh bulrush is a robust, tuber-rooted sedge that forms some of the thickest stands in the mid-to-high brackish marshes of Chesapeake Bay's tributaries, its stout triangular stems and broad leaves towering over shorter marsh grasses. It tolerates regular tidal flooding and moderate salinity better than most freshwater sedges, making it useful for stabilizing eroding shoreline edges and tidal ditch banks. Plant tubers or nursery plugs into saturated to periodically flooded soil in full sun during the growing season; established clumps spread by underground tubers into dense, erosion-resistant colonies. Pair it with smooth cordgrass at the lower marsh edge and saltmeadow cordgrass or black grass higher in the marsh to recreate natural brackish-marsh zonation.

planting.note: Set plugs into consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in spring; divide congested clumps every few years.

directions: Canada rush forms tidy, upright clumps of slender green stems topped in late summer by clusters of small, rounded seed capsules that ripen to a warm copper-brown, adding texture and fall color to a pond edge or rain garden. It is a common component of the marsh-edge and wet-meadow plant communities along Chesapeake Bay's tidal creeks, tolerating both standing water and periodic drying between high tides. Plant nursery plugs into consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to light shade; it is clump-forming rather than aggressively spreading, so it mixes well with other rain garden perennials. Divide congested clumps in spring to maintain vigor and to propagate additional plants for naturalizing wet areas.

planting.note: Plant plugs slightly higher on the marsh grade than cordgrass, in soil that stays moist to seasonally brackish.

directions: Saltmeadow rush forms a low, dense sod of fine, dark green to blackish stems across the high-marsh zone of Chesapeake Bay's brackish shorelines, growing alongside saltmeadow cordgrass and saltgrass in the band of marsh that floods only on the highest tides. Its tough, salt-tolerant root mat is valued for stabilizing soil along living-shoreline plantings and tidal ditch edges where few other perennials establish. Plant nursery plugs in full sun in soil that stays consistently moist to seasonally brackish, setting them slightly higher on the marsh grade than cordgrass so they see less frequent tidal flooding. Cut back old growth in late winter to tidy stands and encourage fresh spring regrowth.
